title: Contact and Deadline
premise: Orsen Galloway, a deniable fixer for an unlisted embassy in Vienna, discovers the safe house he's guarded for three years listed on a real estate site — interior photos included, down to the documents he burned last week. Someone inside the service sold him out, and a professional assassin named Voss is already in the city working the same listing. Over eighteen hours, Orsen must smuggle a defecting analyst's ledger past three governments' handlers and reach a Frankfurt trading floor before markets open, because the ledger proves a sanctioned arms deal that will move billions at the bell. He trades his own anonymity — and his handler's loyalty — for the truth, ending the book exposed, unemployed, and finally belonging to no one but himself.
about_author: E. M. Iversen is the pen name of a former diplomatic security contractor who spent a decade in European capital cities writing reports no one was meant to read. Iversen now lives quietly in Oslo, where the neighbors assume a career in insurance.

chapters.title: The Listing
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. A routine supply run ends when he finds the safe house — his home, his fortress — photographed room by room on a Vienna real estate site, including the room he torched evidence in last Tuesday. The emotional beat is cold vertigo: the rules that protected him just expired.

chapters.title: Housekeeping
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. He sweeps the safe house, finds a micro-camera disguised as a smoke detector, and realizes the photos were taken weeks ago. He burns his contingency identity and calls his handler, Marek, who lies to him badly. Beat: loyalty begins to crack.

chapters.title: The Analyst
chapters.summary: Alternating POV with Ilse Brandt, a disgraced financial analyst who walks into Orsen's dead-drop carrying a ledger of sanctioned arms payments routed through Frankfurt. She chose him because his embassy doesn't exist — no one can disavow what no one admits. Beat: desperate trust between strangers.

chapters.title: Three Flags
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. He tests the ledger against three government contacts and gets three contradictory orders: seize it, destroy it, deliver it. Each order reveals his own service already knew. Beat: the sick clarity of being a disposable asset.

chapters.title: Voss
chapters.summary: Voss's POV, first time. The assassin reviews the same real estate listing as reconnaissance, admires Orsen's tradecraft from a distance, and waits. A near-miss in a subway interchange establishes mutual respect and lethal stakes. Beat: the hunter as a dark mirror of the fixer.

chapters.title: Marek's Choice
chapters.summary: Marek's POV. The handler must choose between burning Orsen to protect the embassy's fiction or helping him, knowing it ends his career. He passes Orsen a Frankfurt contact and a warning: Voss has Ilse's face. Beat: loyalty choosing truth over survival.

chapters.title: Night Train
chapters.summary: Orsen and Ilse's POV, interleaved. The Frankfurt run by rail, trading identities twice, Ilse confessing she sold data once before and this is her penance. Voss boards at Nuremberg. Beat: intimacy forged under pursuit; the price of survival named aloud.

chapters.title: The Bell Tower
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Pre-dawn Frankfurt: Voss corners them in the financial district's service tunnels; Ilse is wounded covering Orsen's escape with the ledger. Beat: grief and fury — the cost is no longer theoretical.

chapters.title: Open
chapters.summary: Climax, Orsen's POV. On the trading floor at 9:00 a.m., he forces a journalist, a regulator, and Marek's embassy contact to witness the ledger simultaneously — too many owners for any one government to bury it. Voss, ordered to silence him amid witnesses, stands down. Beat: truth as a weapon that only works in daylight.

chapters.title: No Return Address
chapters.summary: Resolution, Orsen's POV. Weeks later: the deal collapses, the embassy officially never existed, Marek is quietly retired, and Ilse recovers under a new name. Orsen, finally visible, gets a postcard with no return address — Voss's acknowledgment of a fair fight. Beat: belonging, at last, to himself.
